chapter_text: Mrs. Perera placed a small 1000 µF capacitor on the desk and smiled. “This little part is a capacitor,” she said. “It can store static electric charges.” Nimal connected it carefully to three dry cells with pieces of wire, making sure the terminals were joined correctly. They waited for a few seconds, and Anjali watched the capacitor as if it were a tiny battery holding a secret. When Mrs. Perera removed the dry cells and connected a small LED to the capacitor, the LED glowed for a moment. “That glow happens because the capacitor is discharging,” she explained. “The stored charges are released through the LED.” Nimal leaned closer, and the teacher reminded him that the positive terminal must be connected to the positive side of the LED. The children repeated the activity and saw that the capacitor could be charged again and again. On the board, Mrs. Perera wrote two important words: charging and discharging. “Charging means storing electric charges in the capacitor,” she said, “and discharging means releasing them.” She also showed them the symbol used for a capacitor and pointed out that capacitors come in different sizes. “The amount of charge a capacitor can store is measured in Farads, and microfarad, written µF, is a smaller unit,” she added. Before the bell rang, Anjali looked at the little component with new respect. It was not just a part in a circuit; it was a clever charge keeper. Mrs. Perera told the class that capacitors are found in many electronic devices, and that next time they would look at where such parts appear in radios, televisions, and CFLs.

chapter_text: After lunch, Mrs. Perera brought a small box to the science club table. "Today we are meeting a special part called a capacitor," she said. Nimal watched as she showed a simple circuit with a battery, a bulb, and a tiny capacitor. "A capacitor stores electric charge for a short time, like a tiny energy keeper," she explained. The friends leaned closer when the bulb blinked on and off as the capacitor charged and discharged. Dilani asked why it was not like a battery. Mrs. Perera smiled. "A battery makes electrical energy from chemicals for a longer time, but a capacitor stores charge and releases it quickly." She drew two metal plates with a gap between them. "Inside, the plates collect opposite charges. That stored charge can later flow out and help in things like camera flashes and some electronic timers." Farhan nodded, imagining a flash of light in a split second. To make it real, Mrs. Perera charged a capacitor in the circuit and then disconnected the battery. The bulb still glowed for a short moment, and Sana gasped. "See?" said Mrs. Perera. "The capacitor had saved some electric energy and gave it back little by little." The friends wrote in their notebooks that a capacitor does not create electricity; it stores electrical energy in an electric field between its plates. Before the bell rang, Mrs. Perera pointed to the school gate alarm board. "We will use capacitors again when we learn about timing circuits," she said. Nimal looked at the tiny part with new respect. It was small, but it could hold charge, release energy, and help machines work at the right moment.

chapter_text: On a warm June morning in Weligama, Anjali looked at the sky before school and said, “It feels different today.” Ms. Perera smiled and explained that weather means the short-term condition of the atmosphere, such as temperature, rainfall, humidity, and wind. She pointed to the class table and showed how students record daily weather instead of guessing it from one feeling alone. Kasun read the figures for Colombo from the textbook chart and was surprised. On some days the maximum temperature was the same, and on other days the minimum temperature was the same. Ms. Perera explained that a thermometer measures temperature, and a rain gauge measures rainfall. The class also learned that the day with the highest rainfall was 22.35 mm, so weather can change from one day to the next even in the same month. Then the teacher asked the children to look outside the classroom window. The coconut leaves bent gently, and Anjali said the wind seemed stronger than in the morning. Ms. Perera said that people can also observe wind direction and speed, and that a wind vane and an anemometer are used for this. She reminded them that humidity means the amount of water vapour in the air, which is why some days feel sticky and heavy. By the end of the lesson, the children began their booklet about how people observe weather. Kasun wrote that weather is not the same as climate, because weather changes day by day while climate describes a place over a longer time. Anjali drew a rain gauge beside a bright sun, ready to continue the story of Weligama’s sky tomorrow.

chapter_text: One morning, Aaloka and Nethmi noticed that the sky over the hills looked pale and hazy instead of bright blue. Granny pointed to the swaying jak tree and said, “Today the weather may change.” Aaloka remembered that weather means the condition of the air at a certain time and place, like sunshine, clouds, wind, or rain. By midday, the warm sun had dried the yard, and little wisps of water seemed to disappear from the puddles near the tap. Granny explained that the water was evaporating, turning from liquid into invisible water vapour and rising into the air. “When that vapour cools high up, it can form clouds,” she said, while Nethmi watched a fat cloud grow bigger over the village. Soon a cool breeze moved across the paddy field, and the clouds became darker. Aaloka felt tiny drops on his nose, then a soft rain began to fall on the roof. He laughed and held out his hand. “Weather can change very quickly,” Granny said. “That is why farmers and schoolchildren in Sri Lanka always watch the sky carefully.”

chapter_text: Nethu placed a compass on the bench and watched the needle settle quietly. “It always turns the same way,” she said. Ms. Perera smiled and explained that when a compass is free from other magnets, its north pole points in one direction because Earth itself has a large magnetic field around it. This is called geomagnetism, and the compass needle lines up with that field. Amal held a bar magnet near the compass, and the needle turned at once. “So the compass shows magnetic field direction,” he said. Ms. Perera nodded and added that the direction shown by the compass is called magnetic north. It is not exactly the same as real north; it lies a little to the north-west of it. The students then noticed that no matter how they turned the compass on the table, its needle kept aligning along the same north-south direction. Ms. Perera explained that free magnets and compasses behave this way because Earth’s magnetic field reaches all around us. “That is why sailors and travelers once used compasses to find direction,” she said, tapping the map on the wall. Before the bell rang, Ms. Perera told them one more thing: magnets can lose power if they are exposed to high temperature, strong vibrations, or strong magnetic fields. Nethu carefully placed the compass back in the box and smiled. She had learned that even the Earth is like a giant invisible magnet guiding tiny needles across the classroom.

chapter_text: On a bright Friday afternoon, Nuwan and Ayesha hurried to the school science room, where Ms. Perera had placed a small compass, a bar magnet, and a map of Sri Lanka on the table. “Today,” she said, smiling, “we are learning about geomagnetism—the Earth’s magnetic field.” Ayesha turned the compass slowly, and the needle always settled in one direction. “It is not pointing to a random place,” Ms. Perera explained. “The Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet.” Ms. Perera drew a simple sketch of the Earth and its magnetic field lines. She explained that these invisible lines spread out around our planet and help compass needles point north and south. Nuwan asked, “So the compass is actually feeling the Earth’s magnetism?” “Exactly,” she said. “The needle is a tiny magnet, and it lines up with Earth’s magnetic field.” The children looked at the compass again, now imagining the whole planet around them as a giant invisible magnet. Then Ms. Perera held the bar magnet near the compass. The needle jumped and turned. “This shows that magnets can affect other magnets,” she said. “But Earth’s magnetic field is much bigger, and it protects us too. It helps block some harmful particles from the Sun.” Ayesha remembered hearing about the Sun’s strong energy and was surprised that an invisible force around Earth could help guard life. Before the club ended, Ms. Perera pointed to the map of Sri Lanka and said, “A compass works because of geomagnetism, but remember, magnetic north is not exactly the same as geographic north on a map.” Nuwan nodded carefully, thinking that science was full of hidden directions. As they packed their books, the compass lay quietly on the table, still pointing north, as if the Earth itself was whispering the way forward.

chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon, the Grade 7 science club crowded around the sink in the lab. Ms. Perera held a small turbine made with metal blades fixed to a cork stopper and said, “Let’s see what moving water can do.” When she opened the tap, the water rushed down and the blades spun fast. Kasun laughed, “The water is doing work!” Ms. Perera nodded and explained that moving objects have energy, and the energy in a moving object is called kinetic energy. Nadeesha then pushed a toy car toward a small ball on the table. The ball rolled away after the car hit it, and everyone noticed that work had been done again. “So the moving car had kinetic energy too,” Nadeesha said. Ms. Perera added that flowing water, a moving vehicle, and even a moving pebble are examples of things with kinetic energy. The class wrote down their observations carefully, because this was the first clue that motion itself can carry energy. Next, Ms. Perera pointed to the turbine and asked, “Can we use this moving water to make electricity?” She explained that when energy changes from one form to another, it is called energy transformation. In a windmill, the kinetic energy of wind can be changed into electrical energy by a dynamo; in a hydropower station, the kinetic energy of water is also used to generate electricity. The children imagined the river outside school turning a turbine and lighting up homes far away. Before the bell rang, Ms. Perera smiled and said, “A river at a higher place can flow down and do work, but today we focused on the energy in the moving water itself.” The class left the lab excited, with one more question in their minds: if wind and water can turn motion into useful electricity, what other moving things around them might be hiding kinetic energy?

chapter_text: On a bright afternoon, Nisha carried a plastic bottle filled with marbles to the school science club. Ms. Perera asked the class to place the bottle at the top of the small grassy slope near the playground. When Kasun gave it a gentle push, the bottle rolled faster and faster downhill, making the marbles rattle like tiny drums. "That moving bottle has kinetic energy," Ms. Perera said. "Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving." She explained that the faster the bottle moved, the more kinetic energy it had. Nisha noticed that the bottle at the bottom looked as if it wanted to keep going, and Ms. Perera nodded. "An object with more mass and more speed can have more kinetic energy." Then the teacher placed two balls on the ground: a light rubber ball and a heavier cricket ball. She rolled both balls at the same speed and asked which one would have more kinetic energy. Kasun guessed the cricket ball, because it was heavier, and he was right. The class also saw that when the bottle finally stopped, its kinetic energy had changed into sound, a little heat, and motion in the marbles. As the bell rang, Nisha smiled. She realized that every moving thing around her—an open door swinging in the wind, a running child, even a spinning top—can carry kinetic energy. Next time, she thought, she would watch the school cricket match with new eyes. When the bottle finally stopped, what happened to its kinetic energy? It disappeared completely without changing form. It changed into sound, heat, and motion in the marbles. It turned into light only. It became chemical energy inside the bottle.

chapter_text: Aruni looked at the glowing bulb on the desk and asked, “Sir, why does the bulb get dimmer when we add another part to the circuit?” Mr. Perera smiled and placed a small metal piece beside the wires. “That piece is a resistor,” he said. “The obstacle a conductor gives to the flow of electric current is called resistance. We use the symbol R for resistance, and its unit is the ohm, written as Ω.” Nimal connected the resistor into the circuit, and the ammeter reading became smaller. “So the current has decreased,” he said. Mr. Perera nodded. “Yes. When resistance increases, current decreases. That is why resistors are useful: they help us control the current in a circuit.” He showed them a box of fixed resistors and explained that components made with different resistance values can be added to circuits for this purpose. Then he pointed to the connecting wires. “Copper wires are used for connections because their resistance is very low,” he said. “But metals like nichrome have much higher resistance, so they are used to make resistors. The value of a resistor is often shown by a colour code on it.” Aruni carefully copied the colour bands in her notebook, feeling as if the tiny stripes were secret messages from the wire itself. Before the bell rang, Mr. Perera added, “Remember, current can be controlled by changing resistance.” The students packed up their circuit materials, excited to test more resistors in the next lesson. Outside, the Kandy afternoon was bright, but inside the science room, the little idea of resistance had made the current story even brighter. When the bell rang, Mr. Perera reminded them that the flow of current in a circuit can be adjusted, just like turning a tap. The class left wondering which resistor would make the bulb glow just right in their next experiment.

chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon at St. Anne’s College in Kandy, Nadeesha and Imran were trying to fix a small torch for the science club display. The bulb would glow brightly when they used a short wire, but when they replaced it with a much longer wire, the bulb became dim. Mrs. Perera smiled and said, “That is because the wire’s resistance has changed.” She explained that resistance is the opposition a conductor gives to the flow of electric current. In simple words, it is like the wire’s “difficulty” for electricity to pass through. A longer wire has more resistance because the electrons must travel a bigger distance and meet more obstacles on the way, while a thicker wire usually has less resistance because there is more space for the current to move. Nadeesha compared it to walking through a narrow corridor versus a wide hall, and the class laughed. Mrs. Perera nodded and added that resistance depends on the length, thickness, and material of the conductor. Copper wire is often used in homes because it has low resistance, so it allows current to flow easily. By the end of the period, the torch glowed steadily again, and Imran wrote the important rule in his notebook: longer wire, more resistance; thicker wire, less resistance. Nadeesha tucked the wire into the box and wondered what other school gadgets they could repair using this new idea.

chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon, Ms. Perera placed a red-and-blue cardboard shape on the table. “Today we will build the human heart,” she said. Nethu looked at the model and noticed it was divided into four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. “The right atrium and left atrium are on top, and the right ventricle and left ventricle are below,” Ms. Perera explained, drawing the names carefully on the board. Malith pointed to two flaps made from black paper. “Those are the valves,” he guessed. Ms. Perera nodded. “Yes. The bicuspid valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle, and the tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle. These valves help blood move in the correct direction.” Nethu smiled as the model began to make sense, like a tiny house with doors that open the right way. Then Ms. Perera added two thick tubes to the bottom of the model. “These are the main arteries connected to the ventricles. The aorta starts from the left ventricle, and the pulmonary artery starts from the right ventricle. At the start of each one is a semilunar valve.” She also fixed two thinner tubes at the top. “The superior vena cava and inferior vena cava open into the right atrium, while the left and right pulmonary veins open into the left atrium.” By the time the bell rang, the paper heart stood proudly on the desk. Nethu looked at it one last time and whispered, “So the heart is not just one pump—it has chambers, valves, arteries, and veins all arranged neatly.” Ms. Perera smiled. “Exactly. And next time, we will follow how blood moves through this wonderful organ.”

chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon at Galle Central College, Ms. Perera placed a clay model on the lab table and smiled. “Today,” she said, “we are visiting the human heart.” Nimal leaned closer as Ishani lifted the model’s top half. Inside, they saw that the heart was not one single empty room but a strong muscular organ divided into four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. “The atria receive blood,” Ms. Perera explained, “and the ventricles pump it out with force.” Ishani pointed to a thick wall running down the middle of the model. “Why is the heart split like that?” she asked. “That wall is the septum,” said Ms. Perera. “It keeps oxygen-rich blood and oxygen-poor blood separate.” She then showed them the right side and left side of the heart. “The right side sends blood to the lungs to get oxygen, while the left side sends oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body.” Nimal nodded, imagining the heart as a busy double station. Ms. Perera traced the tiny tube-like openings on the model. “These are blood vessels connected to the heart. The heart has arteries that carry blood away, and veins that bring blood back. The valves act like doors, opening one way only, so blood does not flow backward.” Ishani laughed softly. “So the heart is like a pump with doors and separate rooms!” “Exactly,” said Ms. Perera. “And that smart structure helps it keep blood moving every second of our lives.” As the rain tapped the classroom window, Nimal placed his hand on his chest and felt his own steady beat. The heart seemed small for such an important job, but its chambers, septum, and valves worked together like a carefully planned machine. He knew that in the next lesson, they would discover how this powerful pump actually keeps beating day and night without stopping.
